01 · Foundations

FoundationsBasal Ganglia Anatomy & Circuitry

Key structures: caudate and putamen (together = the striatum), globus pallidus (GPi/GPe), subthalamic nucleus (STN), and substantia nigra (pars compacta [SNc] / pars reticulata [SNr]).

Fig. 1 Basal ganglia direct and indirect pathway circuitry — cortex, striatum, GPe/GPi, STN, SNc, and thalamus Adapted from Albin RL, Young AB, Penney JB. Trends Neurosci. 1989;12:366–375.

Direct pathway (facilitates movement)

Cortex→ Striatum (D1)→ ⊣ GPi / SNr→ disinhibits Thalamus→ Cortex activation

Indirect pathway (inhibits movement)

Cortex→ Striatum (D2)→ ⊣ GPe→ disinhibits STN→ excites GPi / SNr→ ⊣ Thalamus
⚡ Dopamine's dual role Dopamine released from the SNc excites the direct pathway (D1 receptors) and inhibits the indirect pathway (D2 receptors) — so dopamine loss pushes the whole circuit toward less movement.
⚠️ The net effect Loss of dopamine → overactive indirect pathway + underactive direct pathway → excessive GPi output → excessive thalamic inhibition → hypokinesia (Parkinson disease). The opposite imbalance (underactive indirect / overactive direct, or STN/GPi damage) produces hyperkinesia (e.g., chorea, hemiballismus).

Classification Framework

Hypokinetic Disorders

  • Parkinson disease
  • Parkinson-plus syndromes

Hyperkinetic Disorders

  • Tremor
  • Chorea
  • Dystonia
  • Myoclonus
  • Tics
  • Ballism
🔑 How to characterize any movement disorder Activation condition (rest vs. action) · Distribution · Frequency · Rhythm · Suppressibility — run through this checklist for every case below.
02 · Hypokinetic Movement Disorders

HypokineticParkinson Disease

CASE 1The Slow Handwriter

A 63-year-old retired teacher presents with 18 months of progressively smaller handwriting (micrographia). His wife noticed his right hand "shakes when it's resting on his lap" while watching TV, but the shaking stops when he reaches for the remote. Decreased sense of smell for 2 years; acting out his dreams at night. Exam: 4–5 Hz resting "pill-rolling" tremor of the right hand, cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist, decreased arm swing on the right.

  • What are the cardinal motor features here (TRAP)?
  • Which non-motor features are present, and why are they significant?
Reveal Teaching Points

Motor: resting pill-rolling tremor, cogwheel rigidity, and decreased arm swing (early bradykinesia) — classic asymmetric-onset TRAP features.

Non-motor: anosmia and REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) — both are prodromal features that can precede the motor onset of Parkinson disease by years, reflecting early Lewy pathology in the olfactory bulb and brainstem before it reaches the substantia nigra.

Parkinson Disease — Cardinal Features (TRAP)

〜
Tremor
Rest, 4–6 Hz
"Pill-rolling," asymmetric; re-emerges with sustained posture after a brief latency.
🐌
Bradykinesia
Required for diagnosis
Test with rapid alternating movements and finger tapping — decrement in amplitude with repetition is the key finding.
⚙️
Rigidity
Cogwheel & lead-pipe
Cogwheeling reflects rigidity plus superimposed tremor.
🧍
Postural Instability
Late feature
Assessed with the pull test; early falls should raise suspicion for a Parkinson-plus syndrome instead.
🩺 Non-motor features (high-yield) Anosmia (often the earliest symptom), REM sleep behavior disorder, constipation, depression, dementia (late), and orthostatic hypotension. RBD + anosmia can precede motor symptoms by years → prodromal PD.
Fig. 2 Clinical demonstration of the resting, pill-rolling hand tremor characteristic of Parkinson disease Course lecture material

PD — Pathology & Diagnosis

Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the SNc leads to visible depigmentation of the substantia nigra on gross pathology. Surviving and dying neurons accumulate Lewy bodies — intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions composed of aggregated α-synuclein.

Diagnosis is clinical. DaTscan (dopamine transporter SPECT) can confirm a presynaptic dopaminergic deficit when the diagnosis is uncertain — it will be abnormal in PD and Parkinson-plus syndromes, but normal in essential tremor and drug-induced parkinsonism.

Fig. 3 Gross midbrain sections — normal pigmented substantia nigra vs. depigmentation in Parkinson disease Figure 1, ResearchGate (reuse license to be confirmed before any public distribution)
Fig. 4 Microscopic view of the substantia nigra showing dopaminergic neuronal loss Stoker TB, Greenland JC, eds. Parkinson's Disease: Pathogenesis and Clinical Aspects. Codon Publications; 2018. Fig. 1. CC BY 4.0.
Fig. 5 Lewy body — eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion with a pale halo, plus an α-synuclein-positive Lewy neurite Werner CJ et al. Proteome Sci. 2008;6:8. CC BY 2.0; cropped/retouched by Dustfreeworld, Wikimedia Commons.

PD — Treatment

Drug ClassExamplesKey Point
Levodopa / CarbidopaLevodopa + carbidopaMost effective agent available; carbidopa inhibits peripheral DOPA decarboxylase, reducing peripheral side effects (nausea, hypotension)
Dopamine AgonistsPramipexole, ropiniroleCan be used as initial monotherapy in younger patients; watch for impulse control disorders (gambling, hypersexuality, compulsive shopping)
MAO-B InhibitorsSelegiline, rasagilineMild symptomatic benefit by slowing dopamine breakdown
COMT InhibitorsEntacapone, tolcaponeExtend levodopa's effect; tolcapone requires LFT monitoring
AmantadineAmantadineTreats levodopa-induced dyskinesias
AnticholinergicsTrihexyphenidyl, benztropineBest for tremor-predominant disease in younger patients; avoid in elderly (cognitive side effects)
SurgicalDeep brain stimulation (STN or GPi)For motor fluctuations refractory to medical therapy
💊 Long-term levodopa complications "On-off" fluctuations and dyskinesias are complications of long-term levodopa use — amantadine and dose/timing adjustments are the mainstay of managing peak-dose dyskinesias.
CASE 2The Confused Nursing Home Patient

A 78-year-old nursing home resident with schizophrenia treated with haloperidol for 15 years presents with bilateral symmetric bradykinesia, rigidity, and a shuffling gait. No tremor. No anosmia or RBD. DaTscan is normal.

  • What is the diagnosis, and how does it differ from idiopathic PD?
  • Why is the DaTscan normal here?
  • How should this be managed?
Reveal Teaching Points

Diagnosis: drug-induced parkinsonism from chronic dopamine receptor–blocking (typical antipsychotic) therapy. Unlike idiopathic PD, it is typically bilateral and symmetric, tends to lack a prominent resting tremor, and lacks the prodromal non-motor features (anosmia, RBD) of a true synucleinopathy.

Why DaTscan is normal: the nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons themselves are intact — haloperidol blocks postsynaptic D2 receptors rather than destroying presynaptic dopamine terminals, so the presynaptic transporter signal DaTscan measures is preserved.

Management: reduce the dose or switch to a lower-potency/atypical agent (e.g., quetiapine, clozapine) if antipsychotic therapy is still required; symptoms often improve over weeks to months after the offending drug is withdrawn or reduced.

02b · Parkinson-Plus Syndromes

Parkinson-PlusAtypical Parkinsonism

CASE 3The Falling Professor

A 68-year-old professor presents with 1 year of unexplained backward falls. His wife says he stares with a "surprised" expression. Exam: axial rigidity greater than limb rigidity, wide-eyed stare, cannot look downward on command, though his eyes move downward when you tilt his head (doll's eyes intact). Levodopa trial: no improvement.

  • What is the diagnosis?
  • What does "supranuclear" mean here, and why are the doll's eyes intact?
Reveal Teaching Points

Diagnosis: progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) — early backward falls, axial > limb rigidity, vertical (especially downward) gaze palsy, and levodopa unresponsiveness are classic.

"Supranuclear" means the lesion is above the level of the ocular motor nuclei — in the brainstem gaze centers, not the cranial nerve nuclei or nerves themselves. Because the reflex brainstem circuitry (vestibulo-ocular reflex) tested by the doll's-eyes maneuver bypasses the damaged supranuclear pathways, the eyes still move normally with passive head movement even though voluntary vertical gaze is lost.

PSP — Imaging

Fig. 6 "Hummingbird sign" — midsagittal MRI showing midbrain atrophy with preserved pons, giving a hummingbird silhouette Singh D, Shukla R. Ann Indian Acad Neurol. 2009;12(2):133. Fig. 1.
Fig. 7 "Morning glory sign" — axial MRI through the midbrain showing concave lateral tegmental margins Alexiou G, et al. Biomedicines. 2025;13(5):1009. Fig. 2. CC BY 4.0.
CASE 4The Dizzy Fainter

A 58-year-old man presents with 2 years of progressive gait unsteadiness and recurrent syncope. Urinary incontinence and erectile dysfunction. Exam: orthostatic BP drop of 50 mmHg systolic, wide-based ataxic gait, mild bilateral bradykinesia. Levodopa trial: minimal benefit.

  • What is the diagnosis?
  • What distinguishes the underlying pathology from PD?
Reveal Teaching Points

Diagnosis: multiple system atrophy (MSA) — early, severe autonomic failure (orthostatic hypotension, incontinence, erectile dysfunction) plus cerebellar ataxia and only mild parkinsonism, with poor levodopa response.

Pathology: MSA is an α-synucleinopathy, but the α-synuclein aggregates form glial cytoplasmic inclusions (GCIs) in oligodendrocytes rather than the intraneuronal Lewy bodies of PD — a different cell type and a more diffuse, multi-system distribution (striatonigral, olivopontocerebellar, and autonomic pathways), explaining the combination of parkinsonism, cerebellar signs, and dysautonomia.

MSA — Imaging

Fig. 8 "Hot cross bun sign" — axial pontine MRI showing a cruciform hyperintensity from loss of transverse pontocerebellar fibers (MSA-C) Argarrett. Wikimedia Commons; 2020. CC BY-SA 4.0.
Fig. 9 Putaminal rim sign — axial MRI showing a hyperintense rim along the posterolateral putamen (MSA-P) Cureus. 2024;16:e67896. Fig. 2. CC BY 4.0.

Summary: Parkinson-Plus Syndromes

SyndromeKey Distinguishing FeaturesPathologyClassic Imaging
PSPVertical gaze palsy (downgaze), early backward falls, axial rigidity4R tauopathyHummingbird sign; morning glory sign
MSAEarly severe autonomic failure, cerebellar ataxia or parkinsonism, stridorα-synucleinopathy (GCIs)Hot cross bun sign; putaminal rim sign
CBDAsymmetric rigidity + dystonia, alien limb, cortical sensory loss, apraxia4R tauopathyAsymmetric frontoparietal atrophy
DLBVisual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition, RBD, parkinsonismα-synucleinopathy (cortical LBs)Occipital hypometabolism (FDG-PET)
🧠 Board pearl PSP and CBD = tauopathies. MSA and DLB = synucleinopathies. Grouping the four this way makes the pathology column nearly automatic once you know the acronym.
03 · Hyperkinetic Movement Disorders

HyperkineticTremor, Chorea, Ballism, Dystonia, Myoclonus & Tics

CASE 5The Embarrassed Drinker

A 45-year-old woman presents with bilateral hand tremor that has worsened over 10 years. It makes her spill coffee and her handwriting is shaky. The tremor improves after a glass of wine. Her father had a similar tremor. Exam: bilateral, symmetric 6 Hz postural and kinetic tremor of both hands. No bradykinesia, no rigidity, no resting tremor.

  • What is the diagnosis?
  • What is the alcohol response telling you?
  • What is first-line treatment?
Reveal Teaching Points

Diagnosis: essential tremor (ET) — bilateral, symmetric, action (postural/kinetic) tremor with a positive family history and no parkinsonian features.

Alcohol response: transient improvement with alcohol is a classic and fairly specific supporting feature of ET (thought to relate to cerebellar/olivary circuit modulation) — it is not seen in PD tremor.

First-line treatment: propranolol (or another beta-blocker) or primidone.

Board Pearl — ET vs. PD Tremor Comparison

FeatureEssential TremorParkinson Disease Tremor
TypeAction (postural/kinetic)Resting
SymmetryBilateral, symmetricUnilateral/asymmetric
Frequency4–8 Hz4–6 Hz
Alcohol effectImprovesNo effect
BradykinesiaAbsentPresent (required)
Family historyOften positive (~50% AD)Usually sporadic
DaTscanNormalAbnormal

Chorea & Huntington Disease

Chorea: irregular, flowing, non-repetitive movements that migrate unpredictably between body parts. Parakinesia: patients try to incorporate the involuntary movements into purposeful ones, disguising them as voluntary gestures.

CASE 6The Fidgety Banker

A 42-year-old investment banker is brought in for "fidgeting" and personality changes. Over the past year he has become irritable, impulsive, and was fired for poor judgment. His father died in a psychiatric facility at age 55 with "dementia and involuntary movements." Exam: irregular, flowing, non-repetitive movements migrating from face to arms to legs; parakinesia. Cognitive testing: impaired executive function.

  • What is the diagnosis?
  • What genetic mechanism explains earlier onset in his (hypothetical) children?
Reveal Teaching Points

Diagnosis: Huntington disease — the triad of chorea, psychiatric symptoms (personality change, impulsivity), and cognitive decline, plus an autosomal dominant family history, is classic.

Genetic mechanism: anticipation — the CAG repeat in HTT tends to expand further with each generation, especially through paternal transmission (repeat instability is greater during spermatogenesis than oogenesis), producing earlier and more severe disease in offspring.

Huntington Disease — Genetics

Autosomal dominant; chromosome 4p (HTT gene); CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion.

CAG Repeat RangeCategorySignificance
≤26NormalNo disease risk
27–35Intermediate (premutation)No disease in this person, but risk of expansion in offspring
36–39Reduced penetranceMay or may not develop disease
≥40Full penetranceDisease will develop
>60Juvenile HD (Westphal variant)Rigidity > chorea; seizures; more rapid decline

Huntington Disease — Clinical & Pathology

Clinical triad: chorea + dementia + psychiatric symptoms (depression, personality changes). Pathology: selective atrophy of the caudate nucleus (and putamen) from loss of GABAergic medium spiny neurons. Treatment: VMAT2 inhibitors (tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine, valbenazine) for chorea — there is no disease-modifying therapy.

Fig. 10 Caudate and putaminal atrophy with secondary ventricular enlargement ("box-car" lateral ventricles) — prodromal HD vs. control GeneReviews®. University of Washington, Seattle. Fig. 3.

Other Causes of Chorea

🦠
Sydenham Chorea
Post-streptococcal
Anti-basal ganglia antibodies; a manifestation of rheumatic fever.
🤰
Chorea Gravidarum
Pregnancy-associated
Often a recurrence of prior Sydenham chorea, triggered by pregnancy.
🩸
SLE
Antiphospholipid antibodies
Chorea can be a neuropsychiatric manifestation of lupus.
CASE 7The Flinging Arm

A 72-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes and hypertension presents to the ED with sudden onset of violent, large-amplitude flinging movements of his left arm and leg that started 3 hours ago. CT head shows a small lacunar infarct in the right subthalamic nucleus.

  • What is the diagnosis?
  • What is the pathophysiologic mechanism?
  • How is it treated?
Reveal Teaching Points

Diagnosis: hemiballismus, contralateral to the lesion (right STN infarct → left-sided flinging movements).

Mechanism: loss of STN output removes excitatory drive to the GPi, so GPi under-inhibits the thalamus — excessive thalamocortical drive produces the large-amplitude, proximal flinging movements. It is essentially the mirror image of the hypokinetic circuit disturbance in PD.

Treatment: dopamine-receptor blocking agents (antipsychotics such as haloperidol or a VMAT2 inhibitor) for symptomatic control; the underlying vascular risk factors are also addressed, and many cases improve spontaneously over weeks to months.

Hemiballismus — Imaging

Fig. 11 Lacunar infarct involving the subthalamic nucleus, the classic lesion location for contralateral hemiballismus Etemadifar M, et al. Case Rep Med. 2012;2012:768580. Fig. 2.
CASE 8The Twisted Neck

A 50-year-old woman presents with involuntary turning of her head to the left that has worsened over 6 months. She notices it improves when she touches her chin lightly (sensory trick / geste antagoniste). Exam: sustained involuntary rotation of the head to the left with hypertrophy of the right sternocleidomastoid.

  • What is the diagnosis?
  • What is a "sensory trick," and why is it diagnostically useful?
  • What is first-line treatment?
Reveal Teaching Points

Diagnosis: cervical dystonia (spasmodic torticollis) — sustained, patterned muscle contraction producing abnormal head posture, with compensatory hypertrophy of the overactive muscle.

Sensory trick (geste antagoniste): a light tactile stimulus (touching the chin, cheek, or back of the head) that transiently improves the abnormal posture. It is highly characteristic of dystonia and helps distinguish it from other hyperkinetic movements, which don't respond this way.

First-line treatment: botulinum toxin injection into the overactive muscle(s).

Other High-Yield Dystonias

👁️
Blepharospasm
Involuntary eye closure
Focal dystonia of the orbicularis oculi.
✍️
Writer's Cramp
Task-specific dystonia
Triggered only by the specific fine-motor task (e.g., writing).
🧬
DYT1 Dystonia
Early-onset generalized
Autosomal dominant, TOR1A gene; starts in a limb and generalizes; DBS of GPi for refractory cases.
CASE 9The Lip Smacker

A 65-year-old woman with a 20-year history of bipolar disorder treated with haloperidol presents with involuntary, repetitive lip smacking, tongue protrusion, and chewing movements present for 6 months. The movements persist even after haloperidol was reduced. Her psychiatrist asks about treatment options.

  • What is the diagnosis, and what are its risk factors?
  • Which class of drugs would you avoid here (unlike in drug-induced parkinsonism)?
  • What is FDA-approved for treatment?
Reveal Teaching Points

Diagnosis: tardive dyskinesia — orofacial-predominant repetitive movements from chronic dopamine-receptor blockade. Risk factors: cumulative antipsychotic exposure, older age, female sex, and use of first-generation (typical) agents.

Avoid: further dopamine-receptor blocking agents (more antipsychotic, or anticholinergics, which can worsen tardive dyskinesia) — the opposite of drug-induced parkinsonism, where reducing the antipsychotic is the fix but the movement disorder itself isn't made worse by anticholinergics.

FDA-approved treatment: VMAT2 inhibitors — valbenazine and deutetrabenazine — which deplete presynaptic dopamine and reduce the abnormal movements.

Video Reference: Tardive Dyskinesia vs. Tardive Dystonia

CASE 10The Flapping Hands

A 58-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis is admitted for confusion and asterixis. On exam, when asked to hold his arms outstretched with wrists dorsiflexed, there is a bilateral, irregular flapping movement at the wrists.

  • What is this movement called, and how is it classified?
  • What conditions is it classically associated with?
  • How does it differ mechanistically from tremor?
Reveal Teaching Points

Name/classification: asterixis — a form of negative myoclonus (a brief lapse of sustained muscle contraction, rather than an added movement).

Classic associations: hepatic encephalopathy, uremia, and other metabolic/toxic-metabolic encephalopathies (e.g., hypercapnia, drug toxicity).

Mechanism vs. tremor: tremor is a rhythmic, oscillatory active muscle contraction; asterixis instead reflects brief, involuntary silent periods in ongoing tonic muscle activity — the limb "drops" and then corrects, rather than oscillating continuously.

Myoclonus — Bedside Maneuver & Other Pearls

Fig. 15 Bedside maneuver for eliciting asterixis — arms outstretched with wrists dorsiflexed Course lecture material

Cortical myoclonus: focal, stimulus-sensitive — think of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (startle myoclonus + rapidly progressive dementia). Treatment: clonazepam, levetiracetam, valproate.

CASE 11The Blinking Boy

A 10-year-old boy is brought in by his parents for repetitive eye blinking, shoulder shrugging, and throat clearing present for 2 years. He says he feels an "urge" before the movements and can suppress them briefly, but they come back stronger. He also has difficulty paying attention in school and has been diagnosed with ADHD.

  • What is the diagnosis, and what are the diagnostic criteria?
  • What features distinguish tics from other movement disorders?
  • What are the common comorbidities and first-line treatment?
Reveal Teaching Points

Diagnosis: Tourette syndrome. Diagnostic criteria require multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic, present for more than 1 year, with onset before age 18.

Distinguishing features: a premonitory urge preceding the movement, brief voluntary suppressibility (at the cost of a rebound), and stereotyped, repeatable movements — none of which are typical of chorea, dystonia, or myoclonus.

Comorbidities: ADHD and OCD are the two most common. First-line treatment is behavioral therapy (comprehensive behavioral intervention for tics, CBIT); for tics needing pharmacotherapy, alpha-2 agonists (clonidine, guanfacine) are first-line medications, with antipsychotics (e.g., fluphenazine, risperidone, aripiprazole) reserved for more severe or refractory cases.

04 · Special Topics

Special TopicsWilson Disease & Restless Legs Syndrome

CASE 12The Trembling Teen

A 17-year-old boy presents with progressive dysarthria, clumsiness, and a coarse tremor of both arms that worsens when he holds his arms outstretched (wing-beating tremor). Recently found to have elevated transaminases. Personality changes and declining school performance. Slit-lamp exam: golden-brown rings at the corneal limbus bilaterally. Labs: ceruloplasmin 8 mg/dL (normal >20), markedly elevated 24-hour urine copper.

  • What is the diagnosis?
  • What is the underlying genetic/metabolic defect?
  • What is the treatment?
Reveal Teaching Points

Diagnosis: Wilson disease — a young patient with a movement disorder, liver disease, and Kayser-Fleischer rings, plus low ceruloplasmin and elevated urinary copper, is essentially diagnostic.

Underlying defect: autosomal recessive mutation in ATP7B (chromosome 13), which encodes a copper-transporting ATPase. Loss of function impairs biliary copper excretion and incorporation of copper into ceruloplasmin, leading to toxic copper accumulation in the liver, brain (especially basal ganglia), cornea, and kidneys.

Treatment: copper chelation (trientine or penicillamine) and/or zinc (which blocks intestinal copper absorption), plus dietary copper restriction; liver transplantation can be curative in severe hepatic disease.

Wilson Disease — Imaging & Board Pearl

Fig. 16 Kayser-Fleischer ring — golden-brown copper deposition (Descemet's membrane) at the corneal limbus Fred HL, van Dijk HA. Wikimedia Commons. CC BY 3.0.
Fig. 17 Bilateral basal ganglia T2 signal abnormality in Wilson disease (the "face of the giant panda" sign is seen at the midbrain level in some cases) PubMed Central, PMCID: PMC3173909, Fig. 1; Chakraborty S, et al. S Afr J Radiol. 2013;17(3):104. CC BY 4.0.
🧠 Board pearl Must rule out Wilson disease in any young patient (<40–50) presenting with a movement disorder plus liver disease or psychiatric symptoms.

Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS)

🦵
Presentation
Urge to move legs
Worse at rest and in the evening; relieved by movement.
🔗
Associations
Iron deficiency
Check ferritin; also seen with pregnancy, uremia, and peripheral neuropathy.
💊
Treatment
Dopamine agonists
Pramipexole/ropinirole, gabapentin/pregabalin, and iron supplementation if ferritin is low.

"Stump the Class" Challenges

CHALLENGE A

A 70-year-old woman with well-controlled PD on levodopa for 8 years now has involuntary, writhing, dance-like movements of her trunk and limbs that occur 1 hour after each levodopa dose.

Reveal Answer

Levodopa-induced peak-dose dyskinesias. Treat with amantadine or by adjusting the levodopa dosing (smaller, more frequent doses, or switching to a continuous-delivery strategy).

CHALLENGE B

A 55-year-old man presents with progressive asymmetric right arm rigidity and dystonia. He cannot use his right hand to button his shirt, and sometimes his right arm "moves on its own" and grabs objects without his intention. He has ideomotor apraxia and cortical sensory loss in the right hand.

Reveal Answer

Corticobasal degeneration (CBD). Alien limb phenomenon + asymmetric rigidity + apraxia + cortical sensory loss. A 4R tauopathy; MRI shows asymmetric (here, left) frontoparietal atrophy.

CHALLENGE C

A 6-year-old boy presents with progressive rigidity, bradykinesia, seizures, and cognitive decline. His father was diagnosed with Huntington disease at age 35. Genetic testing shows 72 CAG repeats.

Reveal Answer

Juvenile Huntington disease (Westphal variant). Rigidity > chorea, seizures, and rapid decline. This illustrates anticipation with paternal transmission — a massive repeat expansion producing a much earlier, more severe phenotype than the father's.
